# Four Walls Around Factoring: What a Campaign That Found No New Algorithm Actually Learned

*Thirty-three papers set out to find a new way to factor large numbers. None succeeded. This is the story of why that failure was precise enough to be worth writing down.*

---

## The oldest hard problem in your pocket

Take two large primes $p$ and $q$, multiply them, and publish the product $N = pq$. Multiplying is easy: a phone does it for 300-digit numbers in microseconds. Undoing it, recovering $p$ and $q$ from $N$ alone, is believed to be very hard. Much of internet security has rested on that asymmetry for half a century.

What is strange is how little we can prove about it. Nobody has shown that factoring is hard. No unconditional superpolynomial lower bound on factoring is known in any general model of computation. What we have are *upper* bounds, algorithms that are known to work, and a long list of clever ideas that turned out not to help.

Among the deterministic algorithms, the ones that use no random coin flips and are guaranteed to finish, the best known running time is roughly $N^{1/5}$ arithmetic operations, up to logarithmic factors. That is far better than trial division's $N^{1/2}$. It is also far worse than the subexponential running times that randomised and heuristic methods such as the quadratic sieve and the number field sieve reach in practice. The exponent $1/5$ is a ceiling that someone has reached. It is not a floor that anyone has proved.

A research campaign of 33 papers asked a blunt question: **can any of the known families of ideas push below that ceiling, or give a new kind of factoring method at all?** The answer was no, in every case. The useful part is *how* each "no" was obtained. Where possible, a vague failure was replaced by a theorem that says exactly why an idea cannot work.

This article is about four of those theorems. Each is short, each is elementary once you see it, and each rules out a tempting idea for good.

---

## Wall 1: Changing the polynomial doesn't change the primes

### How the quadratic sieve thinks

The quadratic sieve looks for many integers $x$ for which the number
$$Q(x) = x^2 - N$$
breaks completely into small primes. Each such $x$ is called a *relation*. Collect enough of them, combine them with linear algebra over the two-element field, and you get a congruence $X^2 \equiv Y^2 \pmod N$. From that, $\gcd(X - Y, N)$ has a good chance of being a nontrivial factor.

The small primes used for this are called the *factor base*, and each one is a *column* of the linear-algebra matrix. Not every prime can appear. A prime $p$ divides some value $x^2 - N$ exactly when $x^2 \equiv N \pmod p$ has a solution, that is, when $N$ is a *quadratic residue* (a perfect square) modulo $p$. Roughly half of all primes pass this test. They form what we will call the *split set* of $N$.

### The multiple-polynomial trick

In practice, sieving a single polynomial runs out of steam, because $x^2 - N$ grows as $x$ grows. The standard fix, the *multiple-polynomial quadratic sieve*, switches between many polynomials of the form
$$(ax + b)^2 - N \qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad a x^2 + 2bx + c \quad\text{with } b^2 - ac = N.$$
The two forms are linked by the identity $a\,(ax^2 + 2bx + c) = (ax+b)^2 - N$.

At one point the campaign's record claimed that this trick does something more drastic: that it confines the relations to a column set about a *quarter* the size of the factor base, half of what one polynomial gives. If true, that would shrink the matrix and change the cost accounting. Measurement said otherwise. The observed column density was between $0.487$ and $0.505$, which is the same one-half as before.

### The theorem

The explanation turned out to be a clean theorem.

> **Split-Set Theorem.** Let $p$ be a prime that does not divide $a$. Then $p$ divides some value $(ax+b)^2 - N$ if and only if $N$ is a square modulo $p$. The same holds for $ax^2 + 2bx + c$ whenever $b^2 - ac = N$.

The proof takes a few lines. If $p \mid (ax+b)^2 - N$, then $y = ax + b$ is a square root of $N$ modulo $p$. Conversely, if $y^2 \equiv N \pmod p$, then because $a$ is invertible modulo $p$ we can solve $ax + b \equiv y$ for $x$, and that $x$ works. Changing the polynomial only *shifts and rescales* where the roots sit. It cannot create or destroy them.

From this it follows that **no family of polynomials, however large or cleverly chosen, changes the column set.** For a prime coprime to all the leading coefficients, being a column of *some* member of the family is the same as being in the split set. There is also an exact count: for an odd prime $p$, exactly $(p-1)/2$ of the $p - 1$ nonzero residues $N \bmod p$ make $p$ a column. That is a density of exactly one-half, not one-quarter.

A small example: take $p = 7$ and the polynomial $(3x+5)^2 - N$. For $N = 2$, which is a square modulo 7 because $3^2 = 9 \equiv 2$, there are two roots per period, at $x = 2$ (where $11^2 - 2 = 119 = 7 \cdot 17$) and $x = 4$ (where $17^2 - 2 = 287 = 7 \cdot 41$). For $N = 3$, a non-residue, the value is never divisible by 7, whatever $x$ is.

The incorrect "one-quarter" claim was corrected in place in the record. The theorem explains why the measurement came out the way it did.

---

## Wall 2: The Pythagorean shortcut is a loop

### A beautiful tree

Every primitive Pythagorean triple, such as $3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2$ or $5^2 + 12^2 = 13^2$, sits in a single infinite ternary tree discovered by Berggren. Three fixed matrices generate the whole tree from $(3,4,5)$. People have long wondered whether this structure could be used for factoring: put $N$ in a triple, walk the tree, and hope a factor appears along the way.

### The theorem

The campaign proved that the information-carrying part of any such scheme reduces to a single greatest common divisor, and that finding the triple is as hard as factoring.

> **Leg-Channel Theorem.** Let $N > 1$. If $N^2 + b^2 = c^2$ with $b > 0$ and $c - b \neq 1$, then $\gcd(c - b, N)$ is a nontrivial divisor of $N$, strictly between $1$ and $N$.

Here is why. Rewrite the triple as $(c - b)(c + b) = N^2$. Put $u = c - b$ and $v = c + b$, so $u < v$ and $uv = N^2$, which forces $u < N$. If $\gcd(u, N)$ were $1$, then $u$ would be coprime to $N^2$ while dividing it, so $u = 1$, which is excluded. And $\gcd(u, N) \le u < N$. So the gcd lies strictly between $1$ and $N$.

The excluded case $c - b = 1$ is a real triple. For every odd $N = 2k+1$,
$$N^2 + (2k^2+2k)^2 = (2k^2+2k+1)^2,$$
and it tells you nothing. In the other direction, any factorization hands you a nontrivial triple. If $N = de$ with $e = 2m + 1$, then scaling the trivial triple of $e$ by $d$ gives a triple on leg $N$ with $c - b = d$. Putting the two directions together:

> **For odd $N > 1$: $N$ is composite if and only if $N$ is a leg of a Pythagorean triple with $b > 0$ and $c - b \ne 1$.**

So finding a useful triple *is* factoring, in a different form. With $N = 15$ there are four triples:
$$15^2 + 112^2 = 113^2,\quad 15^2 + 36^2 = 39^2,\quad 15^2 + 20^2 = 25^2,\quad 15^2 + 8^2 = 17^2.$$
Their differences $c - b$ are $1, 3, 5, 9$, and the gcds with 15 are $1, 3, 5, 3$. The trivial triple gives nothing, and each of the others gives a factor. Whatever walk through Berggren's tree reaches one of those triples has done the work of factoring along the way. The tree adds no shortcut.

---

## Wall 3: You cannot tell which factor is which

### The "first factor" fallacy

Some proposed side channels aim not to find the factors themselves but to learn *something* about them, such as which one is "first", or which one has a certain Galois or Frobenius property. Under the hood, many such proposals ask a public quantity to distinguish the ordered pair $(p, q)$ from $(q, p)$. But every public quantity computed from $N$ alone is the same for both orderings, since $N = pq = qp$.

### The theorem

The campaign turned this observation into an exact counting theorem.

> **Which-Factor Wall.** Let $S$ be a finite set of secrets with an involution $\sigma$ (a map with $\sigma(\sigma(x)) = x$ that sends $S$ to itself). Let $R$ be a "readout" with $R(\sigma x) = R(x)$, and let $L$ be a "label" with $L(\sigma x) \ne L(x)$ for all $x$ in $S$. Then for **every** decoder $D$, the number of secrets with $D(R(x)) = L(x)$ is at most $|S|/2$.

The proof is a pairing argument. If $D$ is correct on $x$, it is wrong on $\sigma x$: both have the same readout, so $D$ gives the same answer for both, but their labels differ. So $\sigma$ maps the set where $D$ is correct one-to-one into the set where it is wrong. Hence at most half of $S$ can be correct.

In the factoring setting, take $S$ to be the ordered pairs $(p,q)$ of distinct primes from some finite list, $R(p,q) = pq$, and $L(p,q) = p$. **No algorithm, of any running time, can name the first factor correctly on more than half of the pairs.** The bound is also sharp. The decoder "output the least prime factor of $N$" is correct on exactly the pairs with $p < q$, which is exactly half.

The point is that a side channel whose target is order-sensitive while its input is symmetric is blind by construction. Computing harder does not help. The campaign used this, together with an abelianization cap and a "no-pruning" argument for torsors, to close the Galois side-channel family in three independent ways.

---

## Wall 4: Pairs of sets with prime differences

### The open door

One of the campaign's three remaining open questions comes from a divisor-covering approach. The one-dimensional version of that approach was refuted by a published theorem of He and Sahai. The *rank-two* version is still open. Roughly, it asks for two sets $A$ and $B$, each of size about $n^{1/3}$, such that the differences $a - b$ produce about $n^{2/3}$ distinct primes.

No such construction is known. What the campaign proved are two unconditional constraints that any construction must satisfy.

### No slack

> **Capacity.** If every element of a target set $T$ has the form $|a - b|$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$, then $|T| \le |A|\cdot|B|$. If equality holds, distinct pairs $(a, b)$ give distinct differences.

With $|A| = |B| = n^{1/3}$ and $|T| = n^{2/3}$, equality holds, so **every pair has to contribute a different prime**. There is no room for even one repeat.

### Residue rigidity

> **Local Residue Budget.** Suppose every difference $a - b$ (with $a \in A$, $b \in B$) is a prime larger than $m$. Then for every prime $\ell \le m$, the residues of $A$ modulo $\ell$ and the residues of $B$ modulo $\ell$ are disjoint, so
> $$\#(A \bmod \ell) + \#(B \bmod \ell) \le \ell.$$

The reason is short: if some $a \equiv b \pmod \ell$, then $\ell$ divides the prime $a - b$, which is larger than $\ell$, and that is impossible. The case $\ell = 2$ is already strong. All of $A$ has one parity and all of $B$ has the other.

For example, $A = \{0, 6\}$ and $B = \{-5, -11\}$ give differences $5, 11, 11, 17$, all prime. Modulo 2, $A$ lands on $\{0\}$ and $B$ on $\{1\}$. Modulo 3, $A$ lands on $\{0\}$ and $B$ on $\{1\}$. The residues are disjoint, as the theorem requires. The prime 11 appears twice, so this small cover is not injective and would fail the capacity condition at full size. A computer search does find tight examples at small scale. One pair of five-element sets produces 25 differences, all distinct primes. Its residue classes are confined exactly as the budget predicts: modulo 7, the two sets together occupy only 6 of the 7 classes.

These constraints together say that a rank-two construction must sit inside a product of "residue boxes" that avoid the diagonal at every small prime, and must also be perfectly injective. That is exactly the setting of a two-dimensional sieve, and it points to the next step: a global sieve bound that might close this door as well.

---

## The rest of the map

These four theorems are the newly proved part of a larger picture. In the campaign's own summary:

- The deterministic $N^{1/5}$ bound was re-derived three independent ways. In each derivation, the bound comes from the core "motif" of the algorithm. Constraints on the other parts are *slack*, meaning they are not active at the optimum. A general lesson came out of this, the **slack-constraint principle**: tightening a hypothesis moves an exponent only if the corresponding constraint is active at the unconstrained optimum.
- Smoothness-based ideas turned out to be deep, but *orthogonal* to the $N^{1/5}$ record, which contains no smoothness term.
- Transcendence methods (Baker-type bounds on linear forms in logarithms) were closed because of an object mismatch: those bounds never see $N$.
- The class-group route turned out to be priced by the Extended Riemann Hypothesis rather than by Cohen–Lenstra heuristics. A transfer from families to subfamilies that would have helped was measured to fail by a wide margin (a $z$-score of $-41.4$).
- For the quadratic sieve, a **complete-cost rule** reversed an earlier conclusion. You have to count the sieve *plus* the linear algebra. Counting the sieve alone gets the sign of a key trade-off wrong.

The campaign also corrected its own record. A claimed "absolute" density barrier was downgraded to a conjecture. A claim that a certain 2-torsion group is always $C_2$ turned out to be false when $N \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. An inequality had been used in the wrong direction. One of the campaign's own posts was retracted because its numbers had been published before adversarial checking.

---

## Why a negative result can be the right result

It is tempting to treat "no new algorithm" as a non-result. But compare the two possible end states. In one, a dozen ideas have been tried and abandoned, and nobody can say whether they failed for a deep reason or for lack of effort. In the other, each idea is matched with a short theorem showing exactly where it breaks:

- the polynomial family cannot move the column set;
- the Pythagorean triple *is* the factorization;
- no symmetric readout can tell the factors apart better than a coin flip;
- a prime-difference cover must be perfectly injective and residue-rigid.

The second state is much more useful to the next researcher. It shows which doors are closed, why they are closed, and which three are still open: a rank-two separability construction, an upper bound on smooth values of structured polynomial forms, and a class-number bound for a single imaginary quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-pq})$.

The deterministic exponent $1/5$ is still where it was. The map of what lies around it is now considerably more detailed.

# Four Elementary Walls Around Integer Factoring: Split Sets, Pythagorean Legs, Symmetric Readouts, and Rank-Two Prime Covers

**Aristotle**

*October 2026*

---

## Abstract

We report the outcome of a systematic search for new integer-factoring methods. The search covered nine families of approaches: deterministic Lehman-type methods, divisor covers, Pythagorean/Berggren descents, Galois side channels, smoothness, transcendence, class groups, the quadratic sieve, and the number field sieve. It found no new method. In every family, the failure was traced either to a theorem or to a validated measurement. This paper gives complete statements and proofs of four elementary theorems that close specific routes, together with the context that motivates them.

1. **Split-set invariance.** For every prime $p \nmid a$, the prime $p$ divides a value of $(ax+b)^2 - N$ if and only if $N$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$. Consequently no family of multiple-polynomial quadratic sieve (MPQS) polynomials enlarges or shrinks the column set, and the column density is exactly $(p-1)/2$ out of $p-1$. This corrects an earlier claimed density of $\sim 1/4$.
2. **The Pythagorean leg channel.** For every $N > 1$, a triple $N^2 + b^2 = c^2$ with $b > 0$ and $c - b \neq 1$ reveals the nontrivial divisor $\gcd(c-b, N)$. For odd $N$, $N$ is composite if and only if it is the leg of such a triple. Locating a nontrivial triple is therefore equivalent to factoring.
3. **The which-factor wall.** If a readout is invariant under an involution that flips a label, every decoder is correct on at most half of the secrets. For semiprimes, the readout $pq$ and the label "first factor" give a sharp bound of $1/2$, attained by the least-prime-factor decoder.
4. **Rank-two local obstructions.** If all differences $a - b$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$ are primes exceeding $m$, then $A$ and $B$ occupy disjoint residue classes modulo every prime $\ell \le m$. Separately, any cover of a target set $T$ by differences satisfies $|T| \le |A||B|$, with equality forcing injectivity.

We describe algorithms and numerical experiments that illustrate each theorem, and we isolate three open problems that make up the current frontier.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 The state of factoring

Let $N$ be a positive integer, typically a product $N = pq$ of two large primes. The best rigorous deterministic factoring algorithms run in time $N^{1/5 + o(1)}$. This exponent is an *upper bound*. No matching lower bound is known, and no unconditional superpolynomial lower bound for factoring is known in any general model of computation. Heuristic and randomised methods, chiefly the quadratic sieve (QS) and the number field sieve (NFS), are much faster in practice. Their analyses depend on unproved hypotheses about the distribution of smooth numbers, or on probabilistic assumptions.

The campaign reported here asked whether any of the known families of ideas yields a new factoring method, deterministic or otherwise, or pushes the deterministic exponent below $1/5$. The headline answer is negative: **zero new factoring methods were found.** The useful output is a *rigorous characterisation of the frontier*. Each family was closed by an explicit argument, and the arguments sort into a small number of reusable principles.

### 1.2 Summary of family verdicts

We summarise the verdicts to give context. The four theorems proved in this paper are marked with a dagger ($\dagger$). The other entries are reported as findings of the broader programme, with the kind of evidence on which each rests.

| Family | Verdict | Kind of argument |
|---|---|---|
| Deterministic $N^{1/5}$ (Lehman–baby-step/giant-step) | intrinsic to the core motif | three independent re-derivations; the "interior" and "$m$-leg" constraints are slack |
| Divisor-cover (one-dimensional) | refuted | published theorem of He and Sahai (false for parameters $\alpha < 1/2$, $\beta < 3/8$, in particular $(1/3,1/3)$) |
| Divisor-cover (rank two) | open | local obstructions $\dagger$ (Section 6) |
| Pythagorean / Berggren | closed | leg channel is a coordinate gcd and is circular $\dagger$ (Section 4); cost floor $Y^{0.6232}$ |
| Galois / Frobenius side channels | closed in three ways | abelianization cap, which-factor wall $\dagger$ (Section 5), torsor no-pruning |
| Smoothness | deep but orthogonal | no per-instance upper bound; the $N^{1/5}$ record carries no smoothness term |
| Transcendence (Baker, $S$-units) | closed | object mismatch: the relevant effective bounds never involve $N$ |
| Class groups | priced by ERH, not Cohen–Lenstra | family-to-subfamily transfer measured false ($z = -41.4$); $h(-pq)$ is an output, not a cost |
| Quadratic sieve | no decoupling | column space equals split set $\dagger$ (Section 3); complete-cost rule |
| Number field sieve | as closed as QS | column set governed by the degree $d$, not by $N$, but no exploitable excess |

### 1.3 General principles

Several methodological findings came out of the campaign. We state them because they are what make the closures reusable.

- **Slack-constraint principle.** Adding a hypothesis that tightens a constraint moves an optimal exponent only if that constraint is *active* at the unconstrained optimum. Slack constraints can be tightened freely without effect.
- **Complete-cost rule.** The cost of a sieve method is the sieve cost *plus* the cost of linear elimination over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Pricing the sieve alone can reverse the sign of a parameter trade-off.
- **Inequality-direction rule.** A proved ceiling can bound the wrong side of a cost. For example, an inequality of the form $\mathrm{rank} + 1 \le k_{\text{success}}$ bounds the success index from below, so a rank ceiling is not a work bound.
- **Vacuity filter.** Any bound exponential in a rank or set size must be compared with the trivial bound before it is used. In one instance, a published bound turned out to be about $7.3 \times 10^5$ orders of magnitude weaker than doing nothing.
- **No pooling across instances.** A within-pool standard error from pooled instances must not be reported as a $z$-score.
- **Symmetric-readout vacuity.** For an unordered secret and an order-sensitive label, every public-input readout is blind. Section 5 makes this precise.

### 1.4 Corrections to the record

The campaign also corrected statements in its own record:

- a density barrier described as "absolute for any method" was downgraded to conjectured, because a necessary ingredient does not exist;
- the claim that a certain 2-torsion subgroup is $C_2$ for every $N$ is false for $N \equiv 1 \pmod 4$;
- the claimed $\sim 1/4$ multiple-polynomial column density was measured at $0.487$–$0.505$, and Theorem 3.5 below proves the exact value $1/2$;
- the claim $k_{\text{success}} \le Q + 1$ is not a theorem, and the inequality $\mathrm{rank}+1 \le k_{\text{success}}$ had been used in the wrong direction;
- a set of raw experimental figures was retracted because they were published before adversarial verification and could not be reproduced.

### 1.5 Organisation

Section 2 fixes notation. Sections 3–6 state and prove the four theorems. Section 7 describes algorithms and experiments. Section 8 discusses the open frontier, and Section 9 lists future directions.

---

## 2. Preliminaries and notation

Throughout, $p$ and $\ell$ denote primes and $N$ a positive integer. For a prime $p$, $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ is the field with $p$ elements. An element $n \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ is a *square* if $n = y^2$ for some $y \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Note that $0$ counts as a square.

**Definition 2.1 (Split set).** The *split set* of $N$ is the set of primes $p$ such that $N$ is a square modulo $p$.

**Definition 2.2 (Sieve polynomials).** For integers $N, a, b, c$ define
$$V_{N,a,b}(x) = (ax+b)^2 - N, \qquad Q_{a,b,c}(x) = a x^2 + 2bx + c.$$
For $a = 1$, $b = 0$, $V_{N,1,0}(x) = x^2 - N$ is the single quadratic-sieve polynomial.

**Definition 2.3 (Column).** A prime $p$ is a *column* of an integer polynomial $F$ if $p \mid F(x)$ for some integer $x$.

**Definition 2.4 (Nontrivial divisor).** An integer $d$ is a *nontrivial divisor* of $N$ if $d \mid N$ and $1 < d < N$.

**Definition 2.5 (Pythagorean triple).** A triple of integers $(x, y, z)$ is *Pythagorean* if $x^2 + y^2 = z^2$. When $x = N$ we call $N$ the *leg* and write the triple as $(N, b, c)$.

**Lemma 2.6 (Single-polynomial criterion).** A prime $p$ divides $y^2 - N$ for some integer $y$ if and only if $N$ is a square modulo $p$. Moreover, $p \mid y^2 - N$ if and only if $y^2 \equiv N$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

*Proof.* Divisibility by $p$ is the same as vanishing modulo $p$. Every residue class modulo $p$ has an integer representative. $\square$

**Lemma 2.7 (Counting residues).** For an odd prime $p$, exactly $(p-1)/2$ of the nonzero residues modulo $p$ are squares.

*Proof.* The squaring map on $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is a group homomorphism with kernel $\{\pm 1\}$, which has two elements since $p$ is odd. Its image therefore has $(p-1)/2$ elements. $\square$

---

## 3. The multiple-polynomial column set is the split set

### 3.1 Background

In the quadratic sieve, a *relation* is an $x$ for which $x^2 - N$ factors completely over a fixed set of small primes, the factor base. The relations are combined by Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb{F}_2$ into a congruence of squares. Only primes in the split set can divide a value $x^2 - N$ (Lemma 2.6), so in effect the factor base is the split set below a bound.

The multiple-polynomial variant replaces $x^2 - N$ by many polynomials $Q_{a,b,c}$ with $b^2 - ac = N$. They are related to $V_{N,a,b}$ by the identity below. A claim in the record held that this confines relations to a column set of density $\sim 1/4$. We prove that the column set is unchanged.

### 3.2 Results

**Lemma 3.1 (MPQS identity).** If $b^2 - ac = N$, then for every $x$,
$$a \cdot Q_{a,b,c}(x) = V_{N,a,b}(x).$$

*Proof.* $a(ax^2 + 2bx + c) = a^2x^2 + 2abx + ac = (ax+b)^2 - (b^2 - ac)$. $\square$

**Lemma 3.2 (Shift identity).** $V_{N,a,b}(x) = (ax+b)^2 - N$ is the single-polynomial value at the point $y = ax + b$.

**Theorem 3.3 (Multiple-polynomial column criterion).** Let $p$ be a prime with $p \nmid a$, and let $N, b$ be arbitrary integers. Then
$$\exists\, x \in \mathbb{Z}:\ p \mid (ax+b)^2 - N \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N \text{ is a square modulo } p.$$

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) By Lemma 3.2, $y = ax + b$ satisfies $p \mid y^2 - N$, so $N$ is a square modulo $p$ by Lemma 2.6.

($\Leftarrow$) By Lemma 2.6 there is an integer $y$ with $y^2 \equiv N \pmod p$. Since $p \nmid a$, the class of $a$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Put $x_0 = a^{-1}(y - b) \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, and let $x$ be any integer representative of $x_0$. Then $ax + b \equiv y$, so $(ax+b)^2 - N \equiv y^2 - N \equiv 0 \pmod p$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.4 (Reduced form).** If $b^2 - ac = N$ and $p \nmid a$, then $p$ is a column of $Q_{a,b,c}$ if and only if $N$ is a square modulo $p$.

*Proof.* By Lemma 3.1, $p \mid Q_{a,b,c}(x)$ implies $p \mid a Q_{a,b,c}(x) = V_{N,a,b}(x)$. Conversely, if $p \mid V_{N,a,b}(x) = a\,Q_{a,b,c}(x)$ and $p \nmid a$, then $p \mid Q_{a,b,c}(x)$ because $p$ is prime. So the columns of $Q_{a,b,c}$ and $V_{N,a,b}$ coincide, and Theorem 3.3 applies. $\square$

**Theorem 3.5 (No polynomial family changes the column set).** Let $\{(a_i, b_i)\}_{i \in I}$ be any nonempty family of integer pairs, and let $p$ be a prime with $p \nmid a_i$ for all $i$. Then
$$\exists\, i \in I,\ \exists\, x:\ p \mid (a_i x + b_i)^2 - N \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N \text{ is a square modulo } p.$$

*Proof.* The forward direction is Theorem 3.3 applied to the index $i$ that witnesses divisibility. For the backward direction, choose any $i \in I$ (the family is nonempty) and apply Theorem 3.3. $\square$

The index set $I$ is arbitrary: finite, infinite, adaptively chosen, or even dependent on $N$. The only requirement is that $p$ be coprime to all the leading coefficients. Primes dividing some $a_i$ are the usual small set excluded in MPQS practice, and for those primes the polynomial $V_{N,a_i,b_i}$ degenerates to the constant $b_i^2 - N$ modulo $p$.

**Theorem 3.6 (Exact column density).** Let $p$ be an odd prime, $p \nmid a$, and $b$ arbitrary. Then
$$\#\{\, n \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times : \exists\, x,\ p \mid (ax+b)^2 - n \,\} = \frac{p-1}{2}.$$

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.3 the set is exactly the set of nonzero squares modulo $p$. Its size is $(p-1)/2$ by Lemma 2.7. $\square$

**Interpretation.** If $N$ is viewed as a uniformly random nonzero residue modulo each prime of the factor base, each prime is a column with probability exactly $1/2$, whatever the polynomial family. The measured densities $0.487$–$0.505$ agree with this. The claimed $\sim 1/4$ does not.

**Example 3.7.** Let $p = 7$, $a = 3$, $b = 5$. Since $3^2 = 9 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$, the integer $N = 2$ is a square modulo $7$. Over one period $x \in \{0, \dots, 6\}$, $(3x+5)^2 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$ has exactly the two solutions $x = 2$ and $x = 4$: indeed $11^2 - 2 = 119 = 7 \cdot 17$ and $17^2 - 2 = 287 = 7 \cdot 41$. For $N = 3$, a non-residue modulo $7$, there is no solution.

### 3.3 Consequence for the cost accounting

Since the column set cannot be shrunk by the choice of polynomials, the linear-algebra stage of any multiple-polynomial variant works with the same number of potential columns as the single-polynomial sieve. Together with the complete-cost rule (§1.3), this means the benefit of multiple polynomials lies entirely in the *sizes* of the sieved values, not in a smaller matrix. This is the precise sense in which there is no decoupling between the sieve and the column structure.

---

## 4. The Pythagorean leg channel is a coordinate gcd

### 4.1 Background

All primitive Pythagorean triples form a single ternary tree rooted at $(3,4,5)$, generated by three fixed integer matrices (the Berggren tree). This has motivated factoring proposals that place $N$ in a triple and navigate the tree. We show that for triples with leg $N$ the only information-bearing quantity is the coordinate gcd $\gcd(c-b, N)$, and that obtaining a nontrivial triple is equivalent to factoring.

### 4.2 Results

**Lemma 4.1 (Leg factor identity).** If $N, b, c \ge 0$ are integers with $N^2 + b^2 = c^2$, then $b \le c$ and
$$(c - b)(c + b) = N^2.$$

*Proof.* $c^2 - b^2 = N^2 \ge 0$ gives $b^2 \le c^2$, hence $b \le c$ for nonnegative integers. The identity is $c^2 - b^2 = N^2$ factored. $\square$

**Theorem 4.2 (The channel is a coordinate gcd).** Let $N > 1$, $b > 0$, $N^2 + b^2 = c^2$, and $c - b \neq 1$. Then $\gcd(c - b, N)$ is a nontrivial divisor of $N$.

*Proof.* Put $u = c - b$ and $v = c + b$. By Lemma 4.1, $uv = N^2$. Since $b > 0$, $u < v$. Also $u > 0$, since otherwise $N^2 = 0$. If $u \ge N$, then $uv > N \cdot N$ because $v > u \ge N$, a contradiction. Hence $u < N$.

Let $g = \gcd(u, N)$. Clearly $g \mid N$. If $g = 1$, then $u$ is coprime to $N^2$, and since $u \mid N^2$ this forces $u = 1$, contrary to hypothesis. So $g > 1$. Finally $g \le u < N$. $\square$

**Proposition 4.3 (The trivial triple).** For every $k \ge 0$,
$$(2k+1)^2 + (2k^2 + 2k)^2 = (2k^2+2k+1)^2,$$
and this triple has $c - b = 1$. So every odd $N$ is the leg of a triple carrying no information about its factors.

*Proof.* Direct expansion: both sides equal $4k^4 + 8k^3 + 8k^2 + 4k + 1$. $\square$

**Proposition 4.4 (Factorization triple).** For all $d, k \ge 0$,
$$\big(d(d+2k)\big)^2 + \big(2k(d+k)\big)^2 = \big(d^2 + 2kd + 2k^2\big)^2,$$
and the difference of the last two entries is $c - b = d^2$.

*Proof.* Polynomial identity. For the difference, $(d^2 + 2kd + 2k^2) - 2k(d+k) = d^2$. $\square$

So a factorization $N = de$ with $1 < d < e$ and $d \equiv e \pmod 2$ produces a triple with $c - b = d^2 \neq 1$.

**Proposition 4.5 (Scaled trivial triple).** For all $d, m \ge 0$,
$$\big(d(2m+1)\big)^2 + \big(d(2m^2+2m)\big)^2 = \big(d(2m^2+2m+1)\big)^2,$$
with $c - b = d$.

**Theorem 4.6 (Composite $\Leftrightarrow$ nontrivial leg triple).** Let $N > 1$ be odd. Then $N$ has a nontrivial divisor if and only if there are integers $b > 0$ and $c$ with $N^2 + b^2 = c^2$ and $c - b \neq 1$.

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) Write $N = de$ with $d$ a nontrivial divisor, so $1 < d < N$ and $e = N/d > 1$. Since $N$ is odd, $e$ is odd, say $e = 2m+1$ with $m \ge 1$. Proposition 4.5 gives the triple $(N, d(2m^2+2m), d(2m^2+2m+1))$. Its second entry is positive, and $c - b = d \neq 1$.

($\Leftarrow$) This is Theorem 4.2. $\square$

**Example 4.7.** For $N = 15$ the triples with $b > 0$ are
$$15^2 + 112^2 = 113^2,\quad 15^2 + 36^2 = 39^2,\quad 15^2+20^2 = 25^2,\quad 15^2 + 8^2 = 17^2,$$
with $c - b \in \{1, 3, 5, 9\}$ and $\gcd(c-b, 15) \in \{1, 3, 5, 3\}$.

### 4.3 Interpretation

Theorem 4.6 says that "find a nontrivial triple with leg $N$" and "find a nontrivial divisor of $N$" are equivalent problems, with reductions computable by one gcd in one direction and a polynomial formula in the other. Any procedure that walks the Berggren tree, or uses any other triple-generating mechanism, and ends at a nontrivial leg triple has therefore solved the factoring instance. Its cost is at least the cost of factoring. The channel is circular. In the broader programme this is complemented by a cost analysis showing a floor of $Y^{0.6232}$ for tree descents, because the branching rate is smaller than the growth of the entries.

---

## 5. Symmetric readouts and the which-factor wall

### 5.1 Setting

Several proposed side channels (Frobenius elements, Galois actions, quadratic characters) try to extract an *order-sensitive* bit about the factors. Typical examples are "which factor is first" or "which factor has property $X$". The public data, however, is a function of $N = pq$, which is symmetric in $p$ and $q$. We formalise the obstruction abstractly.

**Definition 5.1.** A *symmetric-readout problem* consists of:

- a finite set $S$ of secrets;
- an involution $\sigma: S \to S$, meaning $\sigma(\sigma(x)) = x$;
- a readout $R: S \to Y$ with $R(\sigma x) = R(x)$;
- a label $L: S \to Z$ with $L(\sigma x) \neq L(x)$ for all $x \in S$.

A *decoder* is any function $D: Y \to Z$, with no restriction on its computational complexity.

### 5.2 Results

**Theorem 5.2 (Which-factor wall).** In any symmetric-readout problem and for every decoder $D$,
$$2 \cdot \#\{x \in S : D(R(x)) = L(x)\} \le \# S.$$

*Proof.* Let $T = \{x \in S : D(R(x)) = L(x)\}$. The map $\sigma$ is injective, being its own inverse, so $|\sigma(T)| = |T|$. We claim $T \cap \sigma(T) = \emptyset$. Suppose $x = \sigma(y)$ with $y \in T$ and $x \in T$. Then
$$L(\sigma y) = L(x) = D(R(x)) = D(R(\sigma y)) = D(R(y)) = L(y),$$
which contradicts $L(\sigma y) \neq L(y)$. Since $T \cup \sigma(T) \subseteq S$ and the union is disjoint, $2|T| \le |S|$. $\square$

**Corollary 5.3 (Symmetric-readout vacuity).** If $S \neq \emptyset$, no decoder satisfies $D(R(x)) = L(x)$ for all $x \in S$.

*Proof.* Otherwise $T = S$ and $2|S| \le |S|$, forcing $|S| = 0$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.4 (Semiprime instance).** Let $P$ be a finite set of natural numbers and let $S = \{(p,q) \in P \times P : p \neq q\}$ be the set of ordered pairs of distinct elements. For every function $D: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
$$2 \cdot \#\{(p,q) \in S : D(pq) = p\} \le \#S.$$

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 5.2 with $\sigma(p,q) = (q,p)$, $R(p,q) = pq$, and $L(p,q) = p$. The swap is an involution preserving $S$, $pq = qp$, and $p \neq q$ on $S$. $\square$

**Lemma 5.5 (Balanced orientation).** With $S$ as in Theorem 5.4, $2\cdot\#\{(p,q) \in S : p < q\} = \#S$.

*Proof.* The swap is a bijection between pairs with $p < q$ and pairs with $p > q$, and every pair in $S$ is of one of these two kinds. $\square$

**Theorem 5.6 (The wall is sharp).** If every element of $P$ is prime, the decoder $D(N) = \operatorname{lpf}(N)$, the least prime factor, satisfies
$$2 \cdot \#\{(p,q) \in S : \operatorname{lpf}(pq) = p\} = \#S.$$

*Proof.* For distinct primes $p, q$, the least prime factor of $pq$ is a prime dividing $pq$, hence equal to $p$ or $q$. It is at most each of $p$ and $q$, since both divide $pq$. So $\operatorname{lpf}(pq) = \min(p,q)$, and $\operatorname{lpf}(pq) = p$ exactly when $p < q$. Now apply Lemma 5.5. $\square$

**Example 5.7.** For $P = \{2,3,5,7\}$ there are $12$ ordered pairs. The least-prime-factor decoder is correct on the $6$ increasing ones, and the decoder $N \mapsto N/\operatorname{lpf}(N)$ is correct on the other $6$.

### 5.3 Interpretation

The bound in Theorem 5.2 is *information-theoretic*. It holds for decoders of unbounded computational power. So any side channel whose target is an order-sensitive label of an unordered secret, and whose input is a symmetric function of the secret, is blind: on a uniformly random secret it does no better than a fair coin. In the programme this is one of three independent closures of the Galois side-channel family. The other two are an abelianization cap and a torsor "no-pruning" argument, in which an apparent additional primitive turned out to be a ghost, an artefact that carries no extra information.

---

## 6. Local obstructions for rank-two prime covers

### 6.1 Background

The divisor-cover approach asks for small structured sets whose differences or products cover a large set of primes. Its one-dimensional version is refuted by a published theorem of He and Sahai, which shows the required statement false for exponent parameters $\alpha < 1/2$, $\beta < 3/8$, in particular at $(1/3,1/3)$. The rank-two version is open. It asks for sets $A, B$ with $|A| = |B| \approx n^{1/3}$ whose difference set realises prime mass $\approx n^{2/3}$. We prove two unconditional necessary conditions.

**Definition 6.1.** Finite sets $A, B \subset \mathbb{Z}$ form a *prime-difference pair above $m$* if for all $a \in A$ and $b \in B$, $|a - b|$ is a prime exceeding $m$.

### 6.2 Results

**Lemma 6.2.** Let $\ell \le m$ be prime, and suppose $|a - b|$ is a prime exceeding $m$. Then $a \not\equiv b \pmod \ell$.

*Proof.* If $\ell \mid a - b$, then $\ell$ divides the prime $|a-b|$, so $\ell = |a-b| > m \ge \ell$, a contradiction. $\square$

**Theorem 6.3 (Disjoint residue classes).** If $(A, B)$ is a prime-difference pair above $m$ and $\ell \le m$ is prime, then the residue sets $A \bmod \ell$ and $B \bmod \ell$ are disjoint subsets of $\mathbb{Z}/\ell\mathbb{Z}$.

*Proof.* A common residue would be $a \bmod \ell = b \bmod \ell$ for some $a \in A$, $b \in B$, which Lemma 6.2 rules out. $\square$

**Corollary 6.4 (Local residue budget).** Under the same hypotheses,
$$\#(A \bmod \ell) + \#(B \bmod \ell) \le \ell.$$

*Proof.* The two sets are disjoint subsets of a set with $\ell$ elements. $\square$

**Corollary 6.5 (Parity rigidity).** If $(A,B)$ is a prime-difference pair above $m \ge 2$ and $B \neq \emptyset$, then all elements of $A$ have the same parity, and by symmetry so do all elements of $B$, the opposite one.

*Proof.* Fix $b \in B$. For $a, a' \in A$, Lemma 6.2 with $\ell = 2$ gives $a \not\equiv b$ and $a' \not\equiv b \pmod 2$. In $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ two elements different from the same element are equal, so $a \equiv a' \pmod 2$. $\square$

**Theorem 6.6 (Capacity).** Let $A, B \subset \mathbb{Z}$ be finite and $T \subset \mathbb{N}$ finite. If every $t \in T$ equals $|a - b|$ for some $a \in A$, $b \in B$, then $|T| \le |A|\cdot|B|$.

*Proof.* $T$ is contained in the image of $A \times B$ under $(a,b) \mapsto |a-b|$, and an image has at most as many elements as its domain. $\square$

**Theorem 6.7 (Tight capacity forces injectivity).** If in addition $|T| = |A|\cdot|B|$, then $(a,b) \mapsto |a-b|$ is injective on $A \times B$.

*Proof.* We have $|T| \le |\text{image}| \le |A \times B| = |T|$, so the image has the same size as the domain, and the map is injective. $\square$

**Example 6.8.** $A = \{0, 6\}$, $B = \{-5, -11\}$ give differences $5, 11, 11, 17$, all prime and above $m = 3$. Modulo $2$: $A \mapsto \{0\}$, $B \mapsto \{1\}$. Modulo $3$: $A \mapsto \{0\}$, $B \mapsto \{1\}$. The difference set $\{5, 11, 17\}$ has $3 < 4$ elements, and the cover is not injective because $11$ occurs twice.

### 6.3 Interpretation

At the target parameters $|A| = |B| = n^{1/3}$ and $|T| = n^{2/3}$, the capacity bound is an equality. So every pair must yield a *distinct* prime, and there is no slack at all. Simultaneously, Corollary 6.4 confines $(A \bmod \ell, B \bmod \ell)$ to pairs of disjoint subsets of $\mathbb{Z}/\ell\mathbb{Z}$ for every small $\ell$. If $\omega_\ell$ denotes the number of residue classes used, the proportion of admissible configurations carries a local factor of the form $\prod_{\ell \le m}(1 - \omega_\ell/\ell)$. This is the input of a two-dimensional Selberg sieve. The remaining step towards closing the rank-two door is therefore a global sieve upper bound (Section 9).

---

## 7. Algorithms and numerical experiments

We describe four procedures that illustrate the theorems. All of them are elementary and run in time polynomial in the sizes of their inputs, except where noted.

### 7.1 Column-set computation for a polynomial family

**Input:** $N$, a family $\{(a_i,b_i)\}$, and a factor base of primes.
**Output:** the union of column sets over primes coprime to every $a_i$.

For each prime $p$, skip it if $p \mid a_i$ for some $i$. Otherwise test, for each $i$, whether some $x \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ satisfies $(a_i x + b_i)^2 \equiv N \pmod p$. One period suffices by periodicity. This costs $O(|I| \cdot p)$ per prime. By Theorem 3.5 the answer can be computed in $O(\log p)$ by Euler's criterion $N^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ (or $p \mid N$), independently of the family.

*Experiment.* For a twelve-digit semiprime $N = 1000003 \cdot 999983$, a factor base of the $2261$ odd primes below $20000$ that do not divide $N$, and six random MPQS pairs $(a_i, b_i)$ with entries below $10^6$, the family column set coincided exactly with the split set and with the single-polynomial column set on the common primes. Its empirical density was $1172/2255 \approx 0.520$. For each of nine primes $p \le 101$ and random $(a,b)$ with $p \nmid a$, the number of nonzero $n$ for which $p$ is a column was exactly $(p-1)/2$.

### 7.2 Leg-triple enumeration and the gcd channel

**Input:** $N$. **Output:** all triples $(N, b, c)$ with $b > 0$, and the gcd of each with $N$.

Enumerate divisors $u$ of $N^2$ with $u < N$ and $u \equiv N^2/u \pmod 2$. Set $b = (N^2/u - u)/2$ and $c = (N^2/u + u)/2$. Output $\gcd(c - b, N) = \gcd(u, N)$. The cost is dominated by enumerating divisors of $N^2$, which requires the factorization of $N$, in line with the circularity in Theorem 4.6.

*Experiment.* For every $N \in [3, 400]$, every nontrivial triple yielded a gcd strictly between $1$ and $N$, with no exceptions. For every odd $N \in [3, 999]$, the existence of a nontrivial triple matched compositeness exactly. The converse construction (Proposition 4.5) was checked on $(d,e) = (3,5), (7,11), (101,103)$.

### 7.3 Optimal decoders under a symmetric readout

**Input:** a finite set $P$ of primes. **Output:** the maximum accuracy of any decoder $N \mapsto$ guess for the first factor.

Group the ordered pairs by readout $N = pq$. Each group is $\{(p,q),(q,p)\}$, and the optimal decoder picks one label per group. This gives the exact optimum $|S|/2$, as Theorem 5.2 predicts. *Experiment:* for the $43$ primes in $[7, 200]$, the brute-force optimum was $903/1806 = 1/2$ exactly, the least-prime-factor decoder attained the same value, and a random coin-flip decoder scored $0.4945$.

### 7.4 Greedy search for prime-difference pairs

**Input:** a target size $s$, a threshold $m$, and a range $[0, X)$. **Output:** sets $A$, $B$ of size $s$ forming a prime-difference pair above $m$.

Scan candidates in random order and add each one to the smaller side when this keeps all differences prime and above $m$. This is a heuristic with no guarantee of success. *Experiment:* with $s = 5$, $m = 7$, $X = 3000$, the search found
$$A = \{494, 662, 1352, 1454, 1754\},\quad B = \{31, 1491, 1771, 1813, 2361\},$$
whose $25$ differences are $25$ *distinct* primes, a tight and injective cover. The residue occupancies were $(1,1)$ modulo $2$, $(1,2)$ modulo $3$, $(2,2)$ modulo $5$, and $(3,3)$ modulo $7$, all disjoint and within budget, as required by Corollary 6.4.

---

## 8. Discussion: the frontier

### 8.1 What has and has not been shown

Nothing in this work bears on lower bounds for factoring in general. The deterministic exponent $1/5$ is unchanged and remains an upper bound. What has been shown is that specific mechanisms cannot contribute:

- **polynomial diversity** in the quadratic sieve cannot alter the column set (Theorems 3.3–3.6);
- **Pythagorean structure** on the leg cannot deliver a factor more cheaply than factoring (Theorem 4.6);
- **symmetric public data** cannot determine an order-sensitive label of the factors with accuracy above $1/2$ (Theorems 5.2, 5.6);
- **rank-two prime covers** must be perfectly injective and residue-rigid (Theorems 6.3–6.7).

Each closure is unconditional and elementary. Taken together with the principles of §1.3, they show that the failures were structural and not a matter of insufficient effort.

### 8.2 The three open doors

1. **Rank-two additive separability.** Realise $n^{2/3}$ of prime mass as the difference set of two sets of size $n^{1/3}$, a system overdetermined by a factor $n^{1/3}$. No construction is known. Section 6 gives the necessary local conditions.
2. **Smooth-value upper bounds for structured forms.** An inequality of the shape $\Psi_F(x, y) \le C \cdot x \cdot \prod_i \rho(d_i u)$ for the number of $y$-smooth values of a structured polynomial form $F$, where $\rho$ is the Dickman function and $u = \log x / \log y$. This is the missing ingredient for the smoothness route, and it is open in both directions.
3. **A per-instance class-number bound.** A bound on $h(-pq)$ for a *single* imaginary quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-pq})$, as opposed to averages over families, which currently cannot be reached by enumeration.

---

## 9. Future directions

1. **Residue-box sieve bound for rank-two prime covers.** *Conjecture:* if $A, B \subset [1, X]$ and $A - B$ consists of primes exceeding $m$, then $|A|\cdot|B| \le C\, X^2/(\log X)^2$. Then the rank-two door cannot be reached with $|A| = |B| = n^{1/3}$ inside an interval of length $n^{1/3 + o(1)}$. The local residue budget supplies the local densities for a two-dimensional Selberg sieve.
2. **Exact leg-triple count.** *Conjecture:* for odd $N$, the number of triples $N^2 + b^2 = c^2$ with $b > 0$ is exactly $(\tau(N^2) - 1)/2$, and exactly one of them has $\gcd(c - b, N) = 1$. Lemma 4.1 turns triples into factorizations $uv = N^2$ with $u < v$, and for odd $N$ the parity condition $u \equiv v \pmod 2$ is automatic. Numerically, the count formula holds for all odd $N \le 799$.
3. **Which-factor wall for $k$-factor secrets.** *Conjecture:* for ordered $k$-tuples of distinct primes, readout equal to the product, and label equal to the first coordinate, every decoder is correct on at most a $1/k$ fraction, and the least prime factor attains $1/k$. The symmetric group $S_k$ acts freely on such tuples while preserving the readout, which turns the involution argument into an orbit argument.
4. **Number-field analogue of the split set.** *Conjecture:* in the number field sieve with a fixed degree-$d$ polynomial $f$, changing the family of linear polynomials $a - b\theta$ does not change the set of degree-one primes that can appear. That set is exactly $\{p : f \text{ has a root modulo } p\}$, with density $|G|^{-1}\cdot\#\{\sigma \in G : \sigma \text{ has a fixed point}\}$, where $G$ is the Galois group of $f$. The unit-shift argument of Theorem 3.3 should apply to a root of $f$ modulo $p$.

---

## 10. Conclusion

A broad search for new factoring methods ended without a method. It did end with a map. For each family examined there is an identified obstruction, and for four of them we have given complete elementary proofs. The column set of the quadratic sieve is rigid under change of polynomial. The Pythagorean leg channel is a single gcd and is equivalent to factoring. Symmetric readouts are blind to order-sensitive labels, with the sharp constant $1/2$. Rank-two prime covers must be injective and residue-disjoint at every small prime. The remaining frontier consists of three explicitly stated open problems.

def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """Deterministic trial-division primality test (fine for small n)."""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    r = math.isqrt(n)
    f = 3
    while f <= r:
        if n % f == 0:
            return False
        f += 2
    return True


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """Sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, math.isqrt(n) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i:: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i:: i]))
    return [i for i, v in enumerate(sieve) if v]

    """Least prime factor of n >= 2."""
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return 2
    f = 3
    while f * f <= n:
        if n % f == 0:

        f += 2
    return n

    """Is n a square in Z/pZ (0 counts as a square)?"""
    n %= p
    return any((x * x) % p == n for x in range(p))

    """tau(n), the number of positive divisors."""
    count = 0
    for d in range(1, math.isqrt(n) + 1):
        if n % d == 0:
            count += 1 if d * d == n else 2
    return count

          f"(2 = 3^2 mod 7 is a square)")

          f"(3 is a non-residue mod 7)")

          f"17^2-2 = {17**2-2} = 7*{(17**2-2)//7}")

def leg_triples(N: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """All (b, c) with N^2 + b^2 = c^2, b > 0, via (c-b)(c+b) = N^2."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    N2 = N * N
    for u in range(1, N):
        if N2 % u:
            continue
        v = N2 // u
        if (u + v) % 2 == 0 and u < v:
            out.append(((v - u) // 2, (u + v) // 2))
    return sorted(out, reverse=True)


def factor_from_triple(N: int, b: int, c: int) -> int:
    """The coordinate-gcd channel: gcd(c - b, N)."""
    return math.gcd(c - b, N)

    """Scaled trivial triple of e = 2m+1 by d: leg d*e, with c - b = d."""
    m = (e - 1) // 2

def demo_pythagorean() -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 72)
    print("2. THE PYTHAGOREAN CHANNEL IS A COORDINATE GCD (AND CIRCULAR)")

def decoder_accuracy(P: Sequence[int], D: Decoder) -> Tuple[int, int]:

    pairs = [(p, q) for p in P for q in P if p != q]

    pairs = [(p, q) for p in P for q in P if p != q]

def greedy_prime_diff_pair(size: int, m: int, X: int, seed: int = 0) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """Greedy search for A, B in [0, X) with all |a-b| prime > m (small demo)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    A: List[int] = []
    B: List[int] = []
    cand = list(range(X))

    print(f"  |T| = {len(T)} <= |A||B| = {len(A)*len(B)}")

    demo_pythagorean()
    demo_which_factor()
    demo_rank_two()

     count (tau(N^2) - 1)/2 of leg triples for odd N.

def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """Deterministic trial-division primality test (fine for small n)."""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    r = math.isqrt(n)
    f = 3
    while f <= r:
        if n % f == 0:
            return False
        f += 2
    return True

    """Sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, math.isqrt(n) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i:: i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i:: i]))
    return [i for i, v in enumerate(sieve) if v]


def min_fac(n: int) -> int:
    """Least prime factor of n >= 2."""
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return 2
    f = 3
    while f * f <= n:

        f += 2
    return n

    n %= p

    count = 0

def is_prime_diff_pair(A: Sequence[int], B: Sequence[int], m: int) -> bool:
    return all(is_prime(abs(a - b)) and abs(a - b) > m for a in A for b in B)


def residue_report(A: Sequence[int], B: Sequence[int], l: int) -> Tuple[Set[int], Set[int]]:
    return {a % l for a in A}, {b % l for b in B}


def greedy_prime_diff_pair(size: int, m: int, X: int, seed: int = 0) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """Greedy search for A, B in [0, X) with all |a-b| prime > m (small demo)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    A: List[int] = []
    B: List[int] = []
    cand = list(range(X))
    rng.shuffle(cand)
    for x in cand:
        okA = len(A) < size and all(is_prime(abs(x - b)) and abs(x - b) > m for b in B)
        okB = len(B) < size and all(is_prime(abs(a - x)) and abs(a - x) > m for a in A)
        # always feed the smaller side first, so both sets grow together
        if okB and (len(B) < len(A) or not okA):
            B.append(x)
        elif okA:
            A.append(x)
        if len(A) == size and len(B) == size:
            break
    return sorted(A), sorted(B)


def demo_rank_two() -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 72)
    print("4. RANK-TWO LOCAL OBSTRUCTION: DISJOINT RESIDUES AND NO SLACK")
    print("=" * 72)
    A, B, m = [0, 6], [-5, -11], 3
    diffs = sorted({abs(a - b) for a in A for b in B})
    print(f"A={A}, B={B}: differences {[abs(a-b) for a in A for b in B]} -> set {diffs}")
    print(f"  prime-difference pair above m={m}: {is_prime_diff_pair(A, B, m)}")
    for l in [2, 3]:
        rA, rB = residue_report(A, B, l)
        print(f"  mod {l}: A -> {sorted(rA)}, B -> {sorted(rB)}, disjoint={rA.isdisjoint(rB)}, "
              f"budget {len(rA)}+{len(rB)} <= {l}")
    print(f"  capacity: |T|={len(diffs)} <= |A||B|={len(A)*len(B)} ; not tight, "
          f"and indeed 11 appears twice (not injective)")

    m = 7
    A, B = greedy_prime_diff_pair(size=5, m=m, X=3000, seed=4)
    print(f"\nGreedy search, m={m}: A={A}\n                      B={B}")
    print(f"  prime-difference pair: {is_prime_diff_pair(A, B, m)}")
    for l in [p for p in primes_up_to(m)]:
        rA, rB = residue_report(A, B, l)
        print(f"  mod {l}: #A-classes={len(rA)}, #B-classes={len(rB)}, "
              f"disjoint={rA.isdisjoint(rB)}, sum={len(rA)+len(rB)} <= {l}")
    T = {abs(a - b) for a in A for b in B}
    print(f"  |T| = {len(T)} <= |A||B| = {len(A)*len(B)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_split_set()
    demo_pythagorean()
    demo_which_factor()
    demo_rank_two()

algorithms.name: Family-Independent Column-Set Computation via Euler's Criterion
algorithms.description: Computes the set of factor-base primes that can appear as columns in any multiple-polynomial quadratic sieve run. The naive method checks, for each prime p and each polynomial (ax+b)²−N in the family, one full period x = 0,…,p−1, at cost O(|family|·p) per prime. By the Split-Set Theorem the answer does not depend on the family beyond excluding primes that divide a leading coefficient: p is a column if and only if N is a square mod p. Euler's criterion N^((p−1)/2) ≡ 1 (mod p) decides this with O(log p) modular multiplications. The code implements both methods and checks that they agree. Consequence for the sieve: the linear-algebra matrix has the same potential columns whatever polynomials are used.
algorithms.code:
"""Family-independent column-set computation for the multiple-polynomial quadratic sieve."""
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Iterable, Sequence


def euler_is_square(N: int, p: int) -> bool:
    """N is a square mod the odd prime p (0 counts as a square), via Euler's criterion."""
    n = N % p
    return n == 0 or pow(n, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1


def family_column_set_bruteforce(N: int, family: Sequence[tuple[int, int]],
                                 primes: Iterable[int]) -> set[int]:
    """Union over the family of {p : p | (a x + b)^2 - N for some x}, restricted to
    primes coprime to every leading coefficient.  Cost O(|family| * p) per prime."""
    out: set[int] = set()
    for p in primes:
        if any(a % p == 0 for a, _ in family):
            continue
        if any(any(((a * x + b) ** 2 - N) % p == 0 for x in range(p)) for a, b in family):
            out.add(p)
    return out


def family_column_set_fast(N: int, family: Sequence[tuple[int, int]],
                           primes: Iterable[int]) -> set[int]:
    """Same set in O(log p) per prime: by the split-set theorem the family is irrelevant
    except for excluding primes that divide a leading coefficient."""
    return {p for p in primes
            if all(a % p for a, _ in family) and euler_is_square(N, p)}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import random
    N = 1000003 * 999983
    primes = [p for p in range(3, 3000) if all(p % d for d in range(2, int(p ** 0.5) + 1))]
    rng = random.Random(0)
    fam = [(rng.randrange(1, 10 ** 6), rng.randrange(10 ** 6)) for _ in range(5)]
    slow = family_column_set_bruteforce(N, fam, primes)
    fast = family_column_set_fast(N, fam, primes)
    print("brute force == Euler criterion:", slow == fast, " density:",
          round(len(fast) / len([p for p in primes if all(a % p for a, _ in fam)]), 3))

algorithms.name: Pythagorean Leg-Channel Reductions (Triple ⇄ Factorization)
algorithms.description: Implements both directions of the equivalence between nontrivial Pythagorean triples with leg N and nontrivial factorizations of N. Forward: given N² + b² = c² with b > 0 and c − b ≠ 1, return gcd(c − b, N), which the Leg-Channel Theorem guarantees lies strictly between 1 and N (one gcd, O(log N)). Backward: given N = d·e with e = 2m+1 odd, return the scaled trivial triple (de, d(2m²+2m), d(2m²+2m+1)), which has c − b = d (O(1) arithmetic). Enumerating all triples on leg N requires the divisors u < N of N² with u ≡ N²/u (mod 2), that is, essentially the factorization of N. This is the circularity: no triple-generating mechanism can deliver a nontrivial leg triple more cheaply than factoring.
algorithms.pseudocode:
FACTOR_FROM_TRIPLE(N, b, c):
    require N^2 + b^2 = c^2, b > 0
    u ← c − b
    if u = 1: return NONE          // trivial triple, no information
    return gcd(u, N)               // 1 < gcd < N by the Leg-Channel Theorem

TRIPLE_FROM_FACTOR(d, e):          // N = d·e, e odd
    m ← (e − 1)/2
    return (d·e, d(2m^2+2m), d(2m^2+2m+1))   // c − b = d

ALL_TRIPLES(N):
    for u in divisors of N^2 with u < N and u ≡ N^2/u (mod 2):
        yield ((N^2/u − u)/2, (N^2/u + u)/2)
algorithms.code:
"""The Pythagorean leg channel: triples <-> factorizations, in both directions."""
from __future__ import annotations
import math


def factor_from_leg_triple(N: int, b: int, c: int) -> int | None:
    """Given N^2 + b^2 = c^2 with b > 0, return gcd(c - b, N) if the triple is nontrivial
    (c - b != 1); by the leg-channel theorem this is a divisor strictly between 1 and N."""
    assert N * N + b * b == c * c and b > 0
    u = c - b
    if u == 1:
        return None                      # the trivial triple carries no information
    g = math.gcd(u, N)
    assert 1 < g < N                     # guaranteed by the theorem
    return g


def leg_triple_from_factor(d: int, e: int) -> tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Given N = d*e with e odd, return the scaled trivial triple (N, b, c) with c - b = d."""
    assert e % 2 == 1
    m = (e - 1) // 2
    return d * e, d * (2 * m * m + 2 * m), d * (2 * m * m + 2 * m + 1)


def all_leg_triples(N: int) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    """All (b, c) with N^2 + b^2 = c^2, b > 0, via divisors u < N of N^2 with u = N^2/u mod 2.
    (Needs the divisors of N^2, i.e. essentially the factorization: the channel is circular.)"""
    N2 = N * N
    return [((N2 // u - u) // 2, (N2 // u + u) // 2)
            for u in range(1, N) if N2 % u == 0 and (u + N2 // u) % 2 == 0]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for N in (15, 105, 221, 97):
        facs = sorted({factor_from_leg_triple(N, b, c) for b, c in all_leg_triples(N)} - {None})
        print(N, "triples:", len(all_leg_triples(N)), "factors revealed:", facs)
    L, b, c = leg_triple_from_factor(13, 17)
    print("from 13*17:", (L, b, c), "check:", L * L + b * b == c * c, "c-b =", c - b)

algorithms.name: Maximum-Likelihood Decoder for Symmetric-Readout Problems
algorithms.description: Computes the exact optimal decoder, and its success count, for recovering a label L(x) from a readout R(x) when the secret x is uniform on a finite set S. Group the secrets by readout value and output the most frequent label in each group. This is optimal because the decoder's output can depend only on the readout. When R is invariant under an involution σ that changes the label, each group splits into σ-pairs with distinct labels, so the optimum is at most |S|/2 (the Which-Factor Wall). For ordered pairs of distinct primes with R = pq and L = first coordinate, every group is {(p,q),(q,p)}, and the optimum is exactly 1/2, attained by the least prime factor. Complexity: O(|S|) with hashing.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: finite S, readout R, label L
OUTPUT: optimal decoder D*, optimal success count
groups ← map from readout value to label histogram
for x in S: groups[R(x)][L(x)] += 1
for y in groups: D*(y) ← argmax_z groups[y][z]
best ← Σ_y max_z groups[y][z]
return D*, best
// Theorem: if R∘σ = R and L∘σ ≠ L for an involution σ of S, then best ≤ |S|/2.
algorithms.code:
"""Exact optimal decoder for a symmetric-readout problem (the which-factor wall)."""
from __future__ import annotations
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from typing import Callable, Hashable, Sequence, TypeVar

X = TypeVar("X"); Y = TypeVar("Y", bound=Hashable); Z = TypeVar("Z", bound=Hashable)


def optimal_decoder(S: Sequence[X], R: Callable[[X], Y], L: Callable[[X], Z]) -> tuple[dict[Y, Z], int]:
    """Maximum-likelihood decoder under the uniform distribution on S: for each readout value,
    output the most frequent label among the secrets with that readout.  Returns the decoder
    (as a table) and the number of secrets it decodes correctly, which is the optimum."""
    groups: dict[Y, Counter] = defaultdict(Counter)
    for x in S:
        groups[R(x)][L(x)] += 1
    table = {y: cnt.most_common(1)[0][0] for y, cnt in groups.items()}
    return table, sum(cnt.most_common(1)[0][1] for cnt in groups.values())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    P = [p for p in range(2, 300) if all(p % d for d in range(2, int(p ** 0.5) + 1))]
    S = [(p, q) for p in P for q in P if p != q]
    table, best = optimal_decoder(S, lambda x: x[0] * x[1], lambda x: x[0])
    print(f"optimal accuracy = {best}/{len(S)} = {best / len(S)}   (wall: 1/2)")
    lpf_correct = sum(1 for p, q in S if min(p, q) == p)
    print(f"least-prime-factor decoder = {lpf_correct}/{len(S)}")

algorithms.name: Residue-Admissible Greedy Search for Rank-Two Prime-Difference Pairs
algorithms.description: A heuristic search for sets A and B such that every difference |a − b| is a prime greater than m, with a certificate checker for the two proved necessary conditions. Candidates are scanned in random order and added to the smaller side. Each candidate first passes a cheap local filter derived from the Local Residue Budget (it may not share a residue class mod any prime ℓ ≤ m with the opposite side), then the global primality test on all new differences. The certificate reports the residue occupancies #(A mod ℓ), #(B mod ℓ) and checks their sum against ℓ, compares the number of distinct prime differences with the capacity |A||B|, and reports whether the cover is injective. Cost per candidate: O(π(m)·|side| + |side|·√X) with trial division. The search has no success guarantee; it is meant for exploring small instances of the open rank-two problem.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: target size s, threshold m, range [0, X)
A, B ← ∅, ∅
for x in random permutation of [0, X):
    okA ← |A| < s and ADMISSIBLE(x, against B)
    okB ← |B| < s and ADMISSIBLE(x, against A)
    if okB and (|B| < |A| or not okA): B ← B ∪ {x}
    else if okA: A ← A ∪ {x}
    if |A| = |B| = s: break
return A, B

ADMISSIBLE(x, Other):
    for prime ℓ ≤ m: if ∃ y ∈ Other with x ≡ y (mod ℓ): return FALSE   // residue budget
    return ∀ y ∈ Other: |x − y| is prime and > m

CERTIFICATE(A, B): residue budgets per ℓ ≤ m; |T| vs |A||B|; injectivity

visualizations.name: Column Density Under Random Polynomial Families
visualizations.description: For the semiprime 1000003·999983, plots the fraction of odd primes below a growing bound B that are columns of five random multiple-polynomial families, together with the single polynomial x² − N. All curves coincide (the Split-Set Theorem) and settle around 1/2. The retracted value 1/4 is drawn as a dashed line.
visualizations.code:
"""Column density of the multiple-polynomial quadratic sieve is 1/2 for every polynomial family.

For a fixed semiprime N we draw many random MPQS families (a_i, b_i) and, for growing
factor-base bounds B, plot the fraction of odd primes p < B (coprime to all a_i) that are
columns of the family. Every curve is the same curve: the split-set density, which
settles around 1/2. A dashed line at the retracted value 1/4 is shown for contrast.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import math, random
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def primes_up_to(n: int) -> list[int]:
    s = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1); s[0] = s[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, math.isqrt(n) + 1):
        if s[i]: s[i*i::i] = bytearray(len(s[i*i::i]))
    return [i for i, v in enumerate(s) if v]

def is_column(N: int, a: int, b: int, p: int) -> bool:
    # Equivalent (by the split-set theorem) to Euler's criterion, but computed directly.
    am, bm, Nm = a % p, b % p, N % p
    return any(((am * x + bm) % p) ** 2 % p == Nm for x in range(p))

N = 1000003 * 999983
primes = [p for p in primes_up_to(3000) if p > 2 and N % p]
bounds = list(range(50, 3001, 50))
rng = random.Random(7)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
for trial in range(5):
    fam = [(rng.randrange(1, 10**6), rng.randrange(10**6)) for _ in range(4)]
    dens = []
    for B in bounds:
        usable = [p for p in primes if p < B and all(a % p for a, _ in fam)]
        cols = [p for p in usable if any(is_column(N, a, b, p) for a, b in fam)]
        dens.append(len(cols) / max(1, len(usable)))
    ax.plot(bounds, dens, lw=1.6, alpha=0.8, label=f"random family {trial+1}")
single = [sum(1 for p in primes if p < B and pow(N, (p-1)//2, p) == 1) / max(1, sum(1 for p in primes if p < B)) for B in bounds]
ax.plot(bounds, single, "k:", lw=2.5, label="single polynomial x² − N")
ax.axhline(0.5, color="green", lw=1, label="density 1/2 (theorem)")
ax.axhline(0.25, color="red", ls="--", lw=1, label="retracted claim 1/4")
ax.set_xlabel("factor-base bound B"); ax.set_ylabel("fraction of primes that are columns")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_title("Changing the polynomial family never changes the column set")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("column_density.png", dpi=150)
print("saved column_density.png")

visualizations.name: Every Nontrivial Leg Triple Reveals a Factor
visualizations.description: For each leg N from 3 to 150, one dot per Pythagorean triple N² + b² = c² at height c − b (log scale). Grey dots mark the trivial triple c − b = 1, and coloured dots show the revealed factor gcd(c − b, N). Odd primes have only the grey dot, illustrating that for odd N, composite ⇔ a nontrivial triple exists.
visualizations.code:
"""Pythagorean leg triples and the gcd channel.

For every N from 3 to 150 we enumerate all triples N² + b² = c² with b > 0 and plot one dot
per triple at (N, c − b) on a log scale. Dots are coloured by what gcd(c − b, N) reveals:
grey for the trivial triple (c − b = 1, no information), coloured for nontrivial triples,
each of which reveals a proper factor. Odd primes show only the grey dot: for odd N,
composite ⇔ there is a coloured dot.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import math
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm

def leg_triples(N: int) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    out = []
    for u in range(1, N):
        if (N * N) % u == 0:
            v = N * N // u
            if (u + v) % 2 == 0:
                out.append(((v - u) // 2, (v + u) // 2))
    return out

xs_t, ys_t, xs_n, ys_n, cs = [], [], [], [], []
for N in range(3, 151):
    for b, c in leg_triples(N):
        u = c - b
        if u == 1:
            xs_t.append(N); ys_t.append(u)
        else:
            g = math.gcd(u, N)
            assert 1 < g < N
            xs_n.append(N); ys_n.append(u); cs.append(g)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
ax.scatter(xs_t, ys_t, c="lightgrey", s=14, label="trivial triple (c − b = 1)")
sc = ax.scatter(xs_n, ys_n, c=cs, cmap="viridis", s=14, norm=LogNorm(), label="nontrivial triple")
plt.colorbar(sc, label="revealed factor gcd(c − b, N)")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("leg N"); ax.set_ylabel("c − b")
ax.set_title("Every nontrivial Pythagorean triple on leg N hands over a factor of N")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("leg_triples.png", dpi=150)
print("saved leg_triples.png")

visualizations.name: Histogram of Decoder Accuracies Against the Which-Factor Wall
visualizations.description: Evaluates 3000 random decoders, plus the least-factor, largest-factor and constant decoders, on all ordered pairs of distinct primes up to 200 with readout pq. No accuracy exceeds the red line at 1/2, and the structured decoders that always output a factor sit exactly on it.
visualizations.code:
"""The which-factor wall: accuracy of many decoders never exceeds 1/2.

Secrets are ordered pairs of distinct primes up to 200; the readout is N = p q and the label is
p. We evaluate thousands of random decoders (each readout mapped to one of its two factors with a
biased coin), plus structured ones (least factor, largest factor, constant guesses), and plot a
histogram of accuracies against the theoretical wall at 1/2.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import random
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def primes_up_to(n: int) -> list[int]:
    return [p for p in range(2, n + 1) if all(p % d for d in range(2, int(p**0.5) + 1))]

P = primes_up_to(200)
pairs = [(p, q) for p in P for q in P if p != q]
readouts = sorted({p * q for p, q in pairs})
fac = {p * q: (min(p, q), max(p, q)) for p, q in pairs}
rng = random.Random(3)

def accuracy(guess: dict[int, int]) -> float:
    return sum(1 for p, q in pairs if guess.get(p * q) == p) / len(pairs)

accs = []
for _ in range(3000):
    bias = rng.random()
    g = {N: (fac[N][0] if rng.random() < bias else fac[N][1]) for N in readouts}
    if rng.random() < 0.2:  # sometimes guess garbage
        g = {N: (v if rng.random() < 0.7 else 1) for N, v in g.items()}
    accs.append(accuracy(g))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.hist(accs, bins=60, color="#4c8dff", alpha=0.8, label="random decoders")
for name, g in [("least prime factor", {N: fac[N][0] for N in readouts}),
                ("largest prime factor", {N: fac[N][1] for N in readouts}),
                ("always 3", {N: 3 for N in readouts})]:
    a = accuracy(g); ax.axvline(a, ls=":", lw=1.5); ax.text(a, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9, " " + name, rotation=90, va="top", fontsize=8)
ax.axvline(0.5, color="red", lw=3, label="the wall: 1/2")
ax.set_xlabel("fraction of secrets decoded correctly"); ax.set_ylabel("number of decoders")
ax.set_title("No decoder of the symmetric readout N = pq beats 1/2")
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("which_factor_wall.png", dpi=150)
print("saved which_factor_wall.png", max(accs))

visualizations.name: Residue Boxes of a Tight 5×5 Prime-Difference Cover
visualizations.description: For A = {494, 662, 1352, 1454, 1754} and B = {31, 1491, 1771, 1813, 2361}, draws the residue classes mod 2, 3, 5, 7 occupied by A (blue) and B (gold). They never collide, as the Local Residue Budget requires. A side heat-map shows the 25 differences, all distinct primes, so the capacity bound is attained and the cover is injective.
visualizations.code:
"""Residue boxes of a tight rank-two prime cover.

For the 5×5 prime-difference pair A = {494, 662, 1352, 1454, 1754}, B = {31, 1491, 1771, 1813, 2361}
(all 25 differences are distinct primes above 7), we draw, for each prime ℓ ∈ {2, 3, 5, 7}, the
ℓ residue classes, coloured by whether A (blue) or B (gold) occupies them. The classes never
collide, illustrating the local residue budget #(A mod ℓ) + #(B mod ℓ) ≤ ℓ; a side panel shows the
difference matrix, all of whose entries are distinct primes (capacity bound attained, so injective).
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import math

A = [494, 662, 1352, 1454, 1754]
B = [31, 1491, 1771, 1813, 2361]
ells = [2, 3, 5, 7]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.3, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
for row, l in enumerate(ells):
    ra, rb = {a % l for a in A}, {b % l for b in B}
    for r in range(l):
        col = "#4c8dff" if r in ra else "#f2c879" if r in rb else "#dddddd"
        if r in ra and r in rb: col = "red"
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((r, -row), 0.9, 0.8, color=col))
        ax.text(r + 0.45, -row + 0.4, str(r), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
    ax.text(-0.4, -row + 0.4, f"mod {l}", ha="right", va="center")
    ax.text(l + 0.2, -row + 0.4, f"{len(ra)}+{len(rb)} ≤ {l}", va="center", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(-1.6, 9.5); ax.set_ylim(-3.4, 1); ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("Residue classes: A (blue) and B (gold) never share a class")
M = [[abs(a - b) for b in B] for a in A]
axes[1].imshow([[math.log(x) for x in row] for row in M], cmap="Greens")
for i in range(5):
    for j in range(5):
        axes[1].text(j, i, str(M[i][j]), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_xticks(range(5)); axes[1].set_xticklabels(B); axes[1].set_yticks(range(5)); axes[1].set_yticklabels(A)
axes[1].set_title(f"|a − b|: {len({x for row in M for x in row})} distinct primes = |A|·|B|")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("rank_two_residues.png", dpi=150)
print("saved rank_two_residues.png")

interactive_demos.description: Enter a leg N and see every Pythagorean triple N² + b² = c² with b > 0, computed from the divisors of N², with c − b, gcd(c − b, N) and the factor it reveals. interactive_demos.html:
The Pythagorean Leg Channel: every useful triple is a factorization in disguise

Rewrite N² + b² = c² as (c−b)(c+b) = N². If b > 0 and c−b ≠ 1, then gcd(c−b, N) is a factor strictly between 1 and N. For odd N, N is composite exactly when such a triple exists.
The converse: turn a factorization into a triple
If N = d·e with e = 2m+1 odd, scaling the trivial triple of e by d gives (d e)² + (d(2m²+2m))² = (d(2m²+2m+1))², with c − b = d.
